title: Packing More Into a Sentence
overview: Carry more in fewer sentences. Build a long noun phrase that holds three facts at once, ask the second question that opens up a short answer, and ask politely without turning the words round. Write a rule so it applies to everybody, and notice when a sentence has quietly removed the person responsible.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account of reading contracts, a page about idiom, and a site notice.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Pack several facts about one thing into a single phrase
Ask a second question that makes somebody explain
Ask a stranger for information politely
Write a rule that applies to everybody, not just to you
Notice when a sentence has removed the person responsible
Understand a phrase whose words do not add up to its meaning
Keep going through a long explanation without losing the listener
lectureScript:
This unit is about fitting more into less.
Not writing longer sentences. Carrying more inside the same sentence, which is a different skill and a far more useful one.

The first pattern is genuinely new, and it is the one that changes how your writing looks.
It is called a noun phrase, and it means a noun plus everything attached to it.
English lets you attach things on both sides of the noun, and the two sides take different kinds of thing.
In front go single words. The, a, annual, faulty, three-year, safety.
Behind go whole phrases. On the door. Signed last March. Which we have used for years.
Put them together and you get: the three-year maintenance contract signed last March.
That is one phrase. It holds four separate facts, and it is not a sentence yet.
The rule that keeps you out of trouble is short. Single words in front. Phrases behind.
You cannot say the signed last March three-year contract. English will not carry an action in front of the noun.
And notice where those behind-phrases come from. The contract which was signed last March, with the middle taken out, is the contract signed last March.
So you already knew how to make them. You just have not been shortening them.

The second pattern is about asking.
Levels 1 and 2 gave you question words and do and does, and those get you a first answer.
This is about the second question, which is where the useful information actually lives.
Somebody says the job went badly. That tells you nothing.
In what way. What makes you say that. Can you give me an example. And then what happened.
There is one habit worth breaking here.
If you ask was it the supplier's fault, the person can say no, and the conversation is over.
If you ask whose fault was it, they have to tell you something.
So do not offer a one-word answer unless a one-word answer is what you want.

The third pattern is the politeness move, and it does something strange that you have to watch for.
A direct question turns the verb round. Where is the venue.
Put a polite opening in front, and the turning undoes itself.
Could you tell me where the venue IS.
The inside goes back to statement order, because only the outside is a question now.
Could you tell me where is the venue is the error, and almost every learner makes it for a long time.
With does it is even more striking, because does disappears entirely.
What does it cost becomes do you know what it costs.
Not what does it cost. The does has handed its job back to the main verb, which takes the s again.
And if there is no question word, because it is a yes-or-no question, you need if or whether.
Is it open becomes do you know if it is open.

The fourth pattern is a passive you have met, doing a job you have not seen it do.
Level 2 built it on a production line. The cotton is grown. The bags are made.
Here it is the passive of rules and notices, and there is a real reason rules are written this way.
We check every item is only true while we are working.
Every item is checked is true on anybody's shift, and that is exactly what a rule needs to be.
So the passive is not there to sound official. It is there because a rule outlives the person following it.
Watch two small things. The not goes in the middle: visitors are not allowed.
And the question moves is or are to the front: are candidates told the result.

The fifth pattern is the one to be careful with, and this unit treats it as a reading skill as much as a writing one.
It is said that the site will close.
Read that again and ask the only question that matters. Said by whom.
The sentence will not tell you, and it has been built so that it cannot.
Sometimes that is fine. Every item is checked does not name a doer either, and nobody is hiding.
But mistakes were made is the same grammar doing something else entirely.
The reading in this unit is by somebody who checks contracts, and their whole job is that one question.
A clause said the site would be cleared before work began. It did not say by whom.
The contractor assumed the client. The client assumed the contractor. Nobody cleared it and two days were lost.
Nobody in that story was dishonest. The sentence simply had no person in it.

One last thing, and it is a reading skill rather than a pattern.
English at work is full of phrases whose words do not add up. Snowed under. Touch base. Out of the loop.
You can know every word and still not know what was said, which is what an idiom is.
There is a trick. Stop looking at the words and ask what the speaker wants from you.
If they say they will run it past the client, the words are odd and the purpose is not. They are going to ask.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: To say exactly what something means or what it includes.
words.example: The contract defines what counts as damage.
practice: Define your terms before you argue about them.
Define takes as: damage is defined as any mark.
Its noun is definition.
A well-defined role saves a great deal of trouble.
words.tutor: Define one word from your own trade. Ask the tutor whether the definition was precise.

words.meaning: To say which one it is, out of several.
words.example: Please identify the faulty part.
practice: We have identified three possible causes.
Identify answers which one, define answers what it means.
It takes as: identified as a supplier.
Its noun is identification.
words.tutor: Identify one thing from a group. Ask the tutor whether identify or define was right.

words.meaning: To state something exactly, leaving no room for doubt.
words.example: The order did not specify a colour.
practice: Please specify the size when you order.
Specify is what you do to avoid an argument later.
Its noun is specification, often shortened to spec.
Unspecified means nobody said.
words.tutor: Say what somebody failed to specify. Ask the tutor whether it caused a problem.

words.meaning: To show or suggest something, without stating it outright.
words.example: The figures indicate a fall in demand.
practice: A cracked seal indicates water damage.
Indicate is weaker than show and much weaker than prove.
Its noun is indication.
It suits a report, where you cannot yet be certain.
words.tutor: Say what some evidence indicates. Ask the tutor whether indicate was suitably cautious.

words.meaning: To mention something, or to send somebody to another place.
words.example: The letter refers to an earlier agreement.
practice: Refer takes to: refer to the manual.
They referred me to another department.
Its noun is reference, and note the dropped r.
A reference is also a letter about a former employee.
words.tutor: Say what a document refers to. Ask the tutor to check you said refer TO.

words.meaning: To see or show the difference between two things.
words.example: It is hard to distinguish the two grades.
practice: Distinguish takes between, or from.
You distinguish between A and B, or A from B.
Its adjective is distinct: two distinct kinds.
Distinguished also means respected, which is a separate meaning.
words.tutor: Say what is hard to distinguish. Ask the tutor whether you used between or from correctly.

words.meaning: A group of things of the same kind.
words.example: The form has four categories of fault.
practice: Which category does this fall into?
Category takes into after fall: it falls into category two.
Its plural is categories.
To categorise is the verb.
words.starter: It falls into the category of …
words.tutor: Put something into a category. Ask the tutor whether the category was well chosen.

words.meaning: A kind or sort of something.
words.example: There are two types of contract here.
practice: What type of work do you do?
Type of is followed by a singular noun: type of contract.
Type is the everyday word; category is the formal one.
Typical is the adjective from it.
words.tutor: Name two types of something. Ask the tutor to check the singular after type of.

words.meaning: A part or quality that stands out.
words.example: The main feature of the flat is the light.
practice: This model has three features the old one lacked.
A feature is something you would mention.
It is also a verb: the report features two case studies.
Featureless means with nothing that stands out.
words.tutor: Name the main feature of something. Ask the tutor whether feature or part was right.

words.meaning: One part of something larger, especially something abstract.
words.example: There is an element of risk in every job.
practice: The report has three elements: cause, effect and remedy.
An element is a part of a whole, often an idea.
An element of risk means some, not all.
Elementary means basic, from the same root.
words.tutor: Name an element of something. Ask the tutor whether element or part suited it.

words.meaning: One side of a situation, seen from a particular angle.
words.example: The cost is only one aspect of the problem.
practice: Every aspect of the job has changed.
An aspect is a way of looking, not a physical part.
In this aspect, in this respect: both work.
Do not confuse it with expect.
words.tutor: Describe one aspect of a situation. Ask the tutor whether aspect or element was right.

words.meaning: One of the physical parts a thing is built from.
words.example: A single component had failed.
practice: The components arrive from three suppliers.
A component is physical; an element can be an idea.
Component parts is a common phrase, though it repeats itself.
The stress is on the second part: com-PO-nent.
words.tutor: Name a component of something. Ask the tutor whether component or element was right.

words.meaning: A person who has applied for something.
words.example: Every applicant is interviewed by two people.
practice: There were sixty applicants for four places.
An applicant has applied; a candidate has got through.
It comes from apply, with the y becoming i.
Applications are assessed by a panel.
words.tutor: Say what happens to every applicant somewhere. Ask the tutor to check the passive.

words.meaning: A person being considered for a job or a place.
words.example: Four candidates were shortlisted.
practice: The successful candidate will start in March.
A candidate has usually passed a first stage.
Candidates are informed within two weeks.
It is also used in elections.
words.tutor: Say what the successful candidate does. Ask the tutor to check the future form.

words.meaning: A person or organisation that pays for a professional service.
words.example: The client is told before any extra work begins.
practice: We have about forty regular clients.
A client buys a service; a customer buys goods.
Clients are billed at the end of each month.
Clientele is the whole group of them.
words.tutor: Say what happens to a client in some process. Ask the tutor whether client or customer was right.

words.meaning: A person or firm that provides goods to a business.
words.example: The components arrive from three suppliers.
practice: Our main supplier has raised prices twice.
A supplier supplies; a client buys.
Suppliers are paid within thirty days.
Supply chain is the whole route from maker to buyer.
words.tutor: Say something about a supplier. Ask the tutor whether the sentence was active or passive.

words.meaning: A person who lives in a particular place.
words.example: Residents are notified before any road closure.
practice: Every resident receives a copy of the notice.
A resident lives there; a visitor does not.
It is also an adjective: the resident engineer.
Residence is the noun for the place or the fact.
words.tutor: Say what happens to residents in some process. Ask the tutor to check the passive.

words.meaning: A person taking part in something.
words.example: Participants are asked to arrive by nine.
practice: Each participant is given a number.
A participant takes part; an observer only watches.
It comes from participate, which takes in.
Participants are not told the results.
words.tutor: Say what participants are asked to do. Ask the tutor to check the passive form.

words.meaning: The building and land a business occupies.
words.example: Smoking is not permitted on the premises.
practice: The premises are inspected once a year.
Premises is always plural, even for one building.
The premises ARE, never the premises is.
It is a formal word, common on notices.
words.tutor: Write a notice using on the premises. Ask the tutor to check the verb agrees.

words.meaning: A building or service provided for a particular purpose.
words.example: The facility is closed for maintenance.
practice: The new facility opens in March.
Facilities in the plural often means toilets and washrooms.
A facility is provided; premises are occupied.
Its adjective is facile, which means something else entirely.
words.tutor: Describe a facility. Ask the tutor whether the singular or plural sense was meant.

words.meaning: The place where an event is held.
words.example: The venue has been changed to the town hall.
practice: Participants are told the venue a week before.
A venue is for an event, not for daily work.
It is pronounced VEN-you.
The venue was moved, so it was changed by somebody.
words.tutor: Name a venue and say what happens there. Ask the tutor to check the passive.

words.meaning: A piece of ground where something is, was, or will be built.
words.example: Visitors are not allowed on site without a helmet.
practice: The site was cleared last spring.
On site, with no article, is the fixed phrase.
A site is ground; premises are the built thing.
Do not confuse it with sight or cite.
words.tutor: Write a site rule. Ask the tutor whether you spelled site correctly.

words.meaning: One single thing on a list.
words.example: Each item is checked against the order.
practice: Three items were missing from the delivery.
An item is one entry; a component is one part.
Itemised means listed one by one.
Items are stored in a locked cupboard.
words.tutor: Say what happens to each item. Ask the tutor to check the passive.

words.meaning: A thing made for a particular job, usually small.
words.example: The device is fitted by an engineer.
practice: Every device is tested before it leaves.
A device does a job; an item is just a thing on a list.
Devise is the verb, spelled with an s.
Devices are returned to the supplier if faulty.
words.tutor: Say what happens to a device. Ask the tutor whether you spelled device with a c.

words.meaning: Exact, with no room for doubt.
words.example: Give me the precise figure, not a rough one.
practice: The precise wording matters in a contract.
Precise is about exactness; accurate is about being right.
Its adverb is precisely, which also means exactly so.
Precision is the noun.
words.tutor: Ask for something precise. Ask the tutor whether precise or accurate was right.

words.meaning: Not clearly expressed; leaving too much open.
words.example: The instructions were vague about the deadline.
practice: A vague answer is worse than no answer.
Vague is the opposite of precise.
It is pronounced VAYG, with a silent u.
Vagueness is the noun.
words.tutor: Say what was vague. Ask the tutor whether you spelled vague correctly.

words.meaning: Able to be understood in more than one way.
words.example: The clause is ambiguous and both sides read it differently.
practice: An ambiguous instruction is dangerous on site.
Vague says too little. Ambiguous says two things at once.
Its noun is ambiguity.
The stress is on the second part: am-BIG-you-us.
words.tutor: Say what is ambiguous and why. Ask the tutor whether vague or ambiguous was right.

words.meaning: Stated openly and directly, leaving nothing to be guessed.
words.example: The contract is explicit about who pays.
practice: She gave explicit instructions not to start.
Explicit is said; implicit is only understood.
Its adverb is explicitly.
Explicit is the safer of the two in writing.
words.tutor: Say what a document is explicit about. Ask the tutor to check the preposition.

words.meaning: Understood without being said.
words.example: There was an implicit agreement that nobody would mention it.
practice: The threat was implicit rather than stated.
Implicit is the opposite of explicit.
Implicit in the offer was a deadline.
Its adverb is implicitly.
words.tutor: Describe something implicit. Ask the tutor whether implicit or explicit fitted.

grammar.title: What goes before the noun, and what goes after it
grammar.explanation:
A noun phrase is a noun plus everything attached to it.
English lets you attach things on BOTH sides, and that is how a formal
sentence carries so much in so little space.
This is new. Nothing below this unit builds one.
grammar.rule:
BEFORE the noun, in this order:
determiner + adjective + noun-used-as-adjective + NOUN
the        long        safety                    record
a          three-year  maintenance               contract

AFTER the noun:
a phrase with a preposition   the contract FOR THE ROOF
an -ing phrase                the contract COVERING THE ROOF
an -ed phrase                 the contract SIGNED LAST MARCH
a relative clause             the contract WHICH WE SIGNED

Both sides at once:
the three-year maintenance contract signed last March
  the            -> determiner
  three-year     -> compound adjective
  maintenance    -> noun acting as an adjective
  contract       -> the head noun
  signed last March -> an -ed phrase after it

The -ed and -ing phrases are short relative clauses with the middle removed:
the contract WHICH WAS signed last March -> the contract signed last March
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Build one noun phrase from these three facts.
There is a contract. It lasts three years. We signed it last March.
1. Find the head noun: contract.
2. What can go in FRONT? The length: a three-year contract.
3. What must go AFTER? The signing, because it is a whole action.
4. Shorten which we signed last March to signed last March.
Answer: the three-year contract signed last March.
One phrase, three facts, and no separate sentence needed.
grammar.mistake:
Everything cannot go in front. A whole action has to follow the noun.
No: the signed last March three-year contract.
Yes: the three-year contract signed last March.
Single words go before. Phrases go after.
grammar.tip: Single words in front. Whole phrases behind. The noun sits in the middle.
grammar.practice:
Build ONE noun phrase from each set of facts.
1. There is a report. It is annual. It covers safety.
2. There is a device. It was fitted last year. It is faulty.
3. There are applicants. They applied before Friday.
4. There is a notice. It is on the door. It is about the closure.
5. There is a supplier. They are based locally. We have used them for years.
Now break this one back into two sentences.
6. the three-year maintenance contract signed last March
grammar.answers:
1. the annual safety report
2. the faulty device fitted last year
3. the applicants who applied before Friday, or: the applicants applying before Friday
4. the notice on the door about the closure
5. the local supplier we have used for years
6. We signed a maintenance contract last March. It lasts three years.
In every one, the single words went in front and the phrases went behind.
4 or more right: good.

grammar.title: In what way? Questions that open an answer up
grammar.explanation:
Levels 1 and 2 gave you question words and do and does.
Those get you a FIRST answer. This card is about the second question,
the one that turns a short answer into a useful one.
grammar.rule:
When the answer is too general, ask for the case:
In what way?
Can you give me an example?
What makes you say that?
Such as?

When the answer is too short, ask for the rest:
And then what happened?
What else did they say?
How did that work out?

When you are not sure you followed:
So you are saying that the part was already broken?
Do you mean before or after the delivery?
If I have understood, the client was never told.

A question tag turns a statement into a check, which you already do:
The client was never told, was he?

Notice that half of these are not questions in form at all.
So you are saying that... is a statement, said with a rising voice.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Somebody says: The job went badly. You want the detail.
1. The answer is too general, so ask for the case.
2. In what way? asks them to be specific about HOW.
3. If they are still general, follow with: Can you give me an example?
Answer: In what way? — then, if needed, Can you give me an example?
What happened? would also work, but it asks for a story rather than a reason.
grammar.mistake:
A yes-or-no question closes the answer down.
Weak: Was it the supplier's fault?  (they can say no and stop)
Better: Whose fault was it?  or  What went wrong?
If you want more than a word, do not offer a word as the answer.
grammar.tip: General answer? Ask for an example. Short answer? Ask what happened next.
grammar.practice:
Write a follow-up question for each answer.
1. 'The job went badly.'  (you want to know how)
2. 'They said they would deal with it.'  (you want to know what happened after)
3. 'The supplier is unreliable.'  (you want the evidence)
4. 'It is complicated.'  (you want one case)
Now rewrite each yes-or-no question so it opens the answer up.
5. Was it expensive?
6. Did they apologise?
grammar.answers:
Your wording will differ. Each of yours should refuse a one-word answer.
1. In what way? / What went wrong exactly?
2. And then what happened? / How did that work out?
3. What makes you say that? / Can you give me an example?
4. Such as? / Can you give me an example?
5. How much did it come to?  6. What did they say?
Check yours: could the person answer 5 or 6 with just yes or no? If so, try again.

grammar.title: Could you tell me where it is? The question that stops being a question
grammar.explanation:
There is a polite way to ask, and it does something odd to the word order.
The question inside goes back to STATEMENT order.
Where is it?  ->  Could you tell me where it IS?
This is new, and it is the single most useful politeness move in English.
grammar.rule:
A direct question turns the verb round:
Where is the venue?
What does it cost?
When will they reply?

Put a polite opening in front, and the turning UNDOES itself:
Could you tell me where the venue is?
Do you know what it costs?
I was wondering when they will reply.

The openings:
Could you tell me ...        Do you know ...
I was wondering ...          Would you mind telling me ...
Can I ask ...                I would like to know ...

With a yes-or-no question inside, use IF or WHETHER:
Is it open?  ->  Do you know if it is open?
Did they reply?  ->  Could you tell me whether they replied?

And do and does disappear completely:
What does it cost?  ->  Do you know what it costs?
NOT: Do you know what does it cost?
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Make this polite: What does it cost?
1. Choose an opening: Do you know.
2. Keep the question word: what.
3. Now put the inside back into statement order. It costs.
4. The does has done its job and disappears.
Answer: Do you know what it costs?
Do you know what does it cost? is the error, and it is extremely common.
grammar.mistake:
Learners keep the question order inside, which is the whole thing to unlearn.
No: Could you tell me where is the venue?
Yes: Could you tell me where the venue is?
Only the OUTSIDE is a question. The inside is a statement.
grammar.tip: The polite opening is the question. Everything after it is a statement.
grammar.practice:
Make each one polite, using the opening in brackets.
1. Where is the venue? (Could you tell me)
2. What does it cost? (Do you know)
3. When will they reply? (I was wondering)
4. Is it open on Saturday? (Do you know)
5. Did they receive my application? (Could you tell me)
6. Who is in charge? (I would like to know)
Now correct these two.
7. Do you know where is the site office?
8. Could you tell me what does it include?
grammar.answers:
1. Could you tell me where the venue is?
2. Do you know what it costs?
3. I was wondering when they will reply.
4. Do you know if it is open on Saturday?
5. Could you tell me whether they received my application?
6. I would like to know who is in charge.
7. Do you know where the site office is?
8. Could you tell me what it includes?
Number 6 barely changes, because who was already the subject.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Applications are assessed by a panel: the passive of a rule
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 built the present passive on a production line: the cotton is grown,
the bags are made. The form is the same here and the JOB is different.
This is the passive of rules, procedures and notices, where the doer is
everybody, anybody, or deliberately nobody in particular.
grammar.rule:
is or are + the past form, which you already have.

Rules and procedures:
Applications are assessed by a panel.
Every item is checked against the order.
Residents are notified before any road closure.
Smoking is not permitted on the premises.

The NEGATIVE puts not in the middle:
Visitors are not allowed on site without a helmet.

The QUESTION turns is and are to the front:
Are candidates told the result?
How often is the facility inspected?

Why a procedure uses it: the rule applies whoever is on duty.
We check every item  -> only true when WE are working
Every item is checked -> true always, which is what a rule needs
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Write this as a rule: A panel assesses every application.
1. A rule should hold whoever is doing it, so the passive fits.
2. Move the thing to the front: applications.
3. Plural, and present, so are.
4. assess becomes assessed.
5. Keep by a panel, because the reader needs to know who decides.
Answer: Applications are assessed by a panel.
grammar.mistake:
The not goes between the two pieces, not in front of them.
No: Visitors not are allowed on site.
Yes: Visitors are not allowed on site.
Same for the question: Are visitors allowed, never Visitors are allowed?
grammar.tip: A rule holds whoever is on duty. That is why it takes the passive.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each as a rule, in the passive.
1. A panel assesses every application.
2. We check every item against the order.
3. We notify residents before any road closure.
4. We do not permit smoking on the premises.
5. An engineer fits the device.
Now write the question form.
6. Ask whether candidates are told the result.
7. Ask how often they inspect the facility.
grammar.answers:
1. Applications are assessed by a panel.
2. Every item is checked against the order.
3. Residents are notified before any road closure.
4. Smoking is not permitted on the premises.
5. The device is fitted by an engineer.
6. Are candidates told the result?
7. How often is the facility inspected?
Only 1 and 5 keep the by phrase, because in both the reader needs to know who.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: It is said that: the passive that names nobody at all
grammar.explanation:
There is one more passive, and it is the one to be careful with.
It reports a claim without saying whose claim it is.
It is said that the site will close.
Read that sentence and ask: said by whom? The sentence will not tell you.
grammar.rule:
The shape:
It is said that the site will close.
It is understood that a decision has been made.
It is believed that the fault was known about.
It is thought that numbers will fall.

A second shape moves the subject to the front:
The site is said to be closing.
The fault is known to have been reported.

Where you meet it: news reports, official notices, minutes of meetings.

What it is FOR, honestly:
sometimes the source genuinely does not matter
sometimes the writer does not know
and sometimes it hides who is responsible

The reader's question is always the same one:
It is said that  ->  by whom?
Mistakes were made  ->  by whom?
That question is the whole skill.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Turn this into an impersonal report: People say the site will close.
1. Start with It is, because the real subject is nobody in particular.
2. say becomes said.
3. Add that and the whole claim.
Answer: It is said that the site will close.
Now ask the reader's question. Who says it? The sentence has stopped telling you,
and that is exactly what you have to notice when you meet one.
grammar.mistake:
The it is not optional and it does not refer to anything.
No: Is said that the site will close.
Yes: It is said that the site will close.
That it is a placeholder. English will not start the sentence without it.
grammar.tip: Whenever you meet one, ask by whom. If the text will not say, that is the finding.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one impersonally, starting with It is.
1. People say the site will close.
2. People believe the fault was known about.
3. People understand that a decision has been made.
Now do the opposite. For each one, write the question a careful reader asks.
4. It is thought that numbers will fall.
5. Mistakes were made during the inspection.
6. The client was not informed.
grammar.answers:
1. It is said that the site will close.
2. It is believed that the fault was known about.
3. It is understood that a decision has been made.
4, 5 and 6 all get the same question: BY WHOM?
4. Thought by whom? 5. Made by whom? 6. Not informed by whom?
In 5 and 6 somebody is responsible and the sentence has removed them.
That is not always dishonest, and it is always worth noticing.
5 or more right: good.

readings.title: Reading the Small Print
readings.setting: An office, told by somebody who checks documents for a living
readings.passage:
I read contracts for a living, and almost all of my work is one question.
Who does this sentence say is responsible?
Most of the trouble I see comes from two things: a vague phrase, and a passive with nobody in it.
A clause that says the site will be cleared before work begins looks harmless.
Cleared by whom? The contractor assumed the client. The client assumed the contractor.
Neither of them cleared it, and both of them were reading the same sentence.
The second trap is the word reasonable. Reasonable notice. Reasonable condition. Reasonable cost.
Reasonable means whatever the person reading it wants it to mean, which is another way of saying nothing.
I ask for a number every time, and about half the time I get one.
The clauses that never cause trouble are the explicit ones.
The contractor shall clear the site by 8am on the first day. Nobody has ever argued about that sentence.
It names who, what and when, and it is twenty words long.
Long sentences are not the problem. Sentences with nobody in them are.

readings.title: Under the Weather, and Other Traps
readings.passage:
An idiom is a phrase whose meaning you cannot work out from the words in it.
Under the weather does not mean outdoors. It means slightly ill.
This is why a dictionary sometimes leaves you no better off.
You can know every word in the phrase and still have no idea what was said.
A few that turn up constantly at work:
To be snowed under is to have far too much to do.
To touch base is to make brief contact.
To be on the same page is to share an understanding.
To take something on board is to accept it and act on it.
To be out of the loop is to be left out of the information.
To run something past somebody is to ask their opinion before deciding.
There is a trick worth knowing when you meet one.
Do not look at the words. Look at what the speaker wanted from you.
If somebody says they will run it past the client, the words are strange and the purpose is obvious.
They are going to ask. You do not need the phrase to see that.

readings.title: Site Notice: Conditions of Entry
readings.setting: A board at the gate of a building site
readings.passage:
CONDITIONS OF ENTRY
This notice applies to all persons entering the premises.

1. All visitors are signed in at the gate office. No exceptions are made.
2. Hard hats and high-visibility jackets are worn at all times on site.
3. Deliveries are accepted between 07:30 and 16:00 only.
4. Any damage is reported to the site manager on the day it occurs.
5. Smoking is not permitted anywhere on the premises, including vehicles.
6. Visitors are accompanied at all times by a member of site staff.

It is understood that some deliveries arrive outside these hours.
Drivers are asked to telephone the number below rather than wait at the gate.

Site manager: 0000 000 000
This notice is reviewed every six months.

comprehension.q: What is the one question the writer says almost all of their work comes down to?
comprehension.a: Who does this sentence say is responsible?

comprehension.q: Why did nobody clear the site?
comprehension.a: The sentence did not say who had to, so each side assumed the other.
comprehension.why: The passive had no doer in it, and both parties read it their own way.

comprehension.q: Why does the writer object to the word 'reasonable'?
comprehension.a: Because it means whatever the reader wants it to mean.
comprehension.why: The text says that is another way of saying nothing.

comprehension.q: The writer says long sentences are not the problem. What is?
comprehension.why: The last line, and the twenty-word example just before it proves the point.

comprehension.a: Having far too much to do.

comprehension.q: Somebody says they will run it past the client. What will they do?
comprehension.a: Ask the client's opinion before deciding.
comprehension.why: The definition is given, and the last lines use this exact example.

comprehension.q: Why does the article say a dictionary sometimes does not help?
comprehension.a: Because you can know every word and still not know what the phrase means.
comprehension.why: That is the definition of an idiom the article opens with.

comprehension.q: A delivery arrives at 17:00. What should the driver do?
comprehension.a: Telephone the number on the notice rather than wait at the gate.
comprehension.why: Rule 3 gives the hours, and the paragraph below says what to do outside them.

comprehension.q: Can a visitor walk across the site alone?
comprehension.a: No. Visitors are accompanied at all times by site staff.

comprehension.q: The notice says 'It is understood that some deliveries arrive outside these hours.' Understood by whom?
comprehension.why: That is the impersonal passive: it reports a position without naming who holds it.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Say one long noun phrase instead of three sentences
speaking.instructions:
Each set of facts below becomes ONE noun phrase. Say each one aloud.
1. There is a report. It is annual. It covers safety.
2. There is a device. It was fitted last year. It is faulty.
3. There is a supplier. They are local. We have used them for years.
4. There is a notice. It is on the door. It is about the closure.
A model for the first one:
the annual safety report
Tap the mic. Say all four noun phrases, then use one of them in a full sentence.
Tap again and listen.
Check: did the single words go in FRONT and the phrases BEHIND?
speaking.tutor: Say your four noun phrases and ask the tutor whether anything was in the wrong place.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Where the stress lands in a long noun phrase
speaking.instructions:
A long noun phrase has one main stress, and it is almost never on the last word.
It lands on the word that does the identifying.
Listen and repeat. The capitals show the main stress.
the annual SAFEty report
the faulty DEVICE fitted last year
the three-year MAINtenance contract
the NOtice on the door
Say each one, then say the whole sentence around it.
The annual safety report is published in June.
The faulty device fitted last year has been replaced.
Tap the mic. Say the four phrases and the two sentences.
Tap again and listen.
Check: does one word in each phrase stand out clearly above the rest?
If every word is equally strong, the listener cannot find the point.
speaking.tutor: Say the four phrases and ask the tutor which word it heard as the strongest.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Ask the second question
speaking.instructions:
You will hear a short, unhelpful answer. Ask a question that opens it up.
Say your question aloud after each one.
1. 'The job went badly.'
2. 'They said they would deal with it.'
3. 'The supplier is unreliable.'
4. 'It is complicated.'
5. 'There was a problem with the delivery.'
Models, so you can hear the shape:
In what way? What makes you say that? Can you give me an example?
And then what happened? Such as?
Tap the mic. Ask your five questions. Tap again and listen.
Check: could any of your questions be answered with just yes or no?
If so, that one needs rewriting.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor your five follow-up questions and ask which would get the most out of a reluctant speaker.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Ask it politely
speaking.instructions:
Say each question twice: first direct, then polite.
Remember that the polite version puts the inside back into statement order.
1. Where is the venue?
2. What does it cost?
3. When will they reply?
4. Is it open on Saturday?
5. Did they receive my application?
A model for the first one:
Where is the venue? Could you tell me where the venue is?
Tap the mic. Say all five pairs. Tap again and listen.
Check: in the polite version, did the verb go back after the subject?
Did does disappear completely in number 2?
speaking.tutor: Say your five polite questions and ask the tutor whether the word order was right in each.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Listen: what the clause did not say
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
The clause said the site would be cleared before work began.
It did not say who was to clear it.
The contractor assumed it was the client's job, because the client owned the land.
The client assumed it was the contractor's, because the contractor was doing the work.
Nobody cleared it, and the first two days were lost.
It is understood that both sides acted in good faith.
The clause has since been rewritten to name the contractor.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. What did the clause say would happen?
2. What did it fail to say?
3. Why did the contractor assume it was the client's job?
4. How has the clause been changed?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 the site would be cleared before work began. 2 who was to clear it.
3 because the client owned the land. 4 it now names the contractor.
speaking.tutor: Retell the problem to the tutor in three sentences and ask what you left out.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: explain a procedure
speaking.instructions:
Explain a procedure you know, real or invented: how somebody applies, is checked, is told.
Speak for two minutes.
Use the passive at least five times, because a rule holds whoever is on duty.
Use at least two long noun phrases.
A model of the shape:
Applications are assessed by a panel of two.
Every applicant is told within ten working days.
The successful candidate is sent a three-year contract signed by the manager.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: did you say we and I, or did the rule stand on its own?
Where you kept a by phrase, did the listener need it?
speaking.tutor: Explain the procedure to the tutor and ask where a by phrase was missing that a reader would want.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Five long noun phrases, then a paragraph
writing.prompt:
Build five long noun phrases about a place you know: a workplace, a college, a building.
Each must have at least one thing in front of the noun and one phrase after it.
Then use three of them in a short paragraph.
writing.model:
the annual safety report published every June
the three-year maintenance contract signed last March
the faulty heating unit fitted on the top floor
the local supplier we have used since 2015
the notice on the gate about the new hours

The annual safety report published every June was late this year.
It named the faulty heating unit fitted on the top floor, which nobody had reported.
The local supplier we have used since 2015 replaced it within a week.
writing.length: Five phrases plus a three-sentence paragraph, about 90 to 120 words.
writing.criteria:
All five phrases have something before AND after the noun.
At least two use a shortened relative clause (-ed or -ing) after the noun.
Three of the five appear in the paragraph.
No phrase tries to put a whole action in front of the noun.
writing.support: Write the head noun first, in the middle of the line. Then add to the left, then to the right.
writing.extension: Break one of your phrases back into three separate sentences and say which version you prefer.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Six rules in the passive
writing.prompt:
Write six rules for a place, in the style of Reading 3.
Every rule must be passive. Keep a by phrase only where the reader needs to know who.
One rule must be negative, and one must say what happens outside normal hours.
writing.model:
1. All visitors are signed in at the reception desk.
2. Deliveries are accepted between 08:00 and 17:00 only.
3. Any breakage is reported to the duty manager on the day.
4. Bags are not left unattended in the corridor.
5. Keys are issued by the office and returned the same evening.
6. Deliveries outside these hours are held at the gate until morning.
writing.length: Six numbered rules, about 60 to 90 words.
writing.criteria:
All six rules passive, with is or are and a past participle.
At least one negative, with not between the two pieces.
by used at most twice, and only where the reader needs it.
No rule says we or I.
writing.support: Write each rule actively first — We sign in all visitors — then remove the we.
writing.extension: Add two questions a visitor might ask about your rules, in the passive question form.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Six polite questions
writing.prompt:
You are enquiring about a course, a job or a venue.
Write six polite questions, each using a different opening.
Two of them must be yes-or-no questions inside, so they will need if or whether.
writing.model:
Could you tell me when the next course starts?
Do you know what the full cost includes?
I was wondering whether places are still available.
Would you mind telling me who assesses the applications?
I would like to know how long the decision usually takes.
Can I ask if the fee is payable in advance?
writing.criteria:
Six different openings used.
Every inside question in STATEMENT order.
No do or does left inside.
Two questions use if or whether.
writing.support: Write the six direct questions first, then put an opening in front and fix the order.
writing.extension: Turn one of them back into a direct question and say when you would use each version.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Rewrite a clause so nobody can argue
writing.prompt:
Below are three clauses with nobody in them. Rewrite each one so it names who, what and when.
Invent whatever detail you need.
a) The site will be cleared before work begins.
b) Reasonable notice will be given.
c) Any damage is to be made good.
Then write two sentences saying why the original of one of them caused trouble.
writing.model:
a) The contractor shall clear the site by 8am on the first day.
b) The client shall give the contractor at least ten working days' notice in writing.
c) The party causing the damage shall repair it within fourteen days of reporting.

The first clause never said who was to clear the site.
Each side assumed the other, nobody did it, and two days were lost.
writing.length: Three clauses plus two sentences, about 80 to 110 words.
writing.criteria:
Each rewritten clause names a person or party, an action and a time.
No vague word left: reasonable, appropriate, promptly, as soon as possible.
The two sentences explain the consequence, not just the fault.
The rewrites may be longer than the originals; that is expected.
writing.support: Ask the three questions in order: who, what exactly, and by when.
writing.extension: Find a real notice near you and name one sentence in it that does not say who.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Build the noun phrase
activities.instructions:
Build ONE noun phrase from each set of facts.
1. There is a report. It is annual. It covers safety.
2. There is a device. It was fitted last year. It is faulty.
3. There are applicants. They applied before Friday.
4. There is a notice. It is on the door. It is about the closure.
5. There is a supplier. They are local. We have used them for years.
6. There is a contract. It lasts three years. It covers maintenance.
Now break these back into separate sentences.
7. the faulty heating unit fitted on the top floor
8. the local supplier we have used since 2015
activities.answers:
1. the annual safety report
2. the faulty device fitted last year
3. the applicants who applied before Friday (or: applying before Friday)
4. the notice on the door about the closure
5. the local supplier we have used for years
6. the three-year maintenance contract
7. A heating unit was fitted on the top floor. It is faulty.
8. The supplier is local. We have used them since 2015.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the head noun in the middle of the line first, then build outwards in both directions.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Open the answer up
activities.instructions:
Write a follow-up question for each unhelpful answer.
1. 'The job went badly.'
2. 'They said they would deal with it.'
3. 'The supplier is unreliable.'
4. 'It is complicated.'
5. 'There was a problem with the delivery.'
Now rewrite each yes-or-no question so it cannot be answered with one word.
6. Was it expensive?
7. Did they apologise?
8. Is the client happy?
activities.answers:
Your wording will differ. The test is whether a one-word answer is still possible.
1. In what way? 2. And then what happened? 3. What makes you say that?
4. Can you give me an example? 5. What went wrong exactly?
6. How much did it come to? 7. What did they say? 8. What has the client said?
Check each of yours: if the person could say yes and stop, rewrite it.
activities.solo: Write your question, then write the shortest answer somebody could give. If it is one word, try again.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Make it polite
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each one using the opening in brackets.
1. Where is the venue? (Could you tell me)
2. What does it cost? (Do you know)
3. When will they reply? (I was wondering)
4. Is it open on Saturday? (Do you know)
5. Did they receive my application? (Could you tell me)
6. Who is in charge? (I would like to know)
7. How long does the decision take? (Can I ask)
Now correct these.
8. Do you know where is the site office?
9. Could you tell me what does it include?
activities.answers:
1. Could you tell me where the venue is?
2. Do you know what it costs?
3. I was wondering when they will reply.
4. Do you know if it is open on Saturday?
5. Could you tell me whether they received my application?
6. I would like to know who is in charge.
7. Can I ask how long the decision takes?
8. Do you know where the site office is?
9. Could you tell me what it includes?
Number 6 hardly changes, because who was already the subject of its own clause.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Say each one aloud before writing. The wrong order usually sounds wrong before it looks wrong.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Turn a procedure into rules
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each one as a rule, in the passive. Drop we and I.
1. A panel assesses every application.
2. We check every item against the order.
3. We notify residents before any road closure.
4. We do not permit smoking on the premises.
5. An engineer fits the device.
6. We accept deliveries between 07:30 and 16:00.
Now write the question form.
7. Ask whether candidates are told the result.
8. Ask how often they inspect the facility.
activities.answers:
1. Applications are assessed by a panel.
2. Every item is checked against the order.
3. Residents are notified before any road closure.
4. Smoking is not permitted on the premises.
5. The device is fitted by an engineer.
6. Deliveries are accepted between 07:30 and 16:00.
7. Are candidates told the result?
8. How often is the facility inspected?
Only 1 and 5 keep a by phrase. In the rest, naming the doer adds nothing.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write each rule, then read it aloud and ask whether it would still be true on somebody else's shift.

activities.title: Practice 5 — By whom?
activities.instructions:
For each sentence, write the question a careful reader asks, and say whether it matters.
1. It is said that the site will close.
2. Mistakes were made during the inspection.
3. The client was not informed.
4. It is understood that a decision has been made.
5. The site will be cleared before work begins.
6. Every item is checked against the order.
activities.answers:
All six get the same question: BY WHOM?
1. Said by whom? Matters: a rumour and an announcement are not the same.
2. Made by whom? Matters a great deal. This is the classic evasion.
3. Not informed by whom? Matters: somebody had that duty.
4. Understood by whom? Matters: who has decided, and do they have the authority?
5. Cleared by whom? Matters most of all — this is the clause from Reading 1.
6. Checked by whom? Does NOT matter: the rule holds whoever is on duty.
Number 6 is the point of the exercise. A missing doer is not automatically a fault.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Write the question beside each, then mark M where it matters and N where it does not.

activities.title: Practice 6 — What did they actually mean?
activities.instructions:
Each line uses an idiom from Reading 2. Write what the speaker means in plain words.
1. 'I am completely snowed under this week.'
2. 'I will run it past the client on Thursday.'
3. 'I think we are all on the same page now.'
4. 'I have been out of the loop since I was away.'
5. 'We will take that on board.'
6. 'I will touch base with you on Monday.'
activities.answers:
1. I have far too much to do this week.
2. I will ask the client's opinion on Thursday before deciding.
3. I think we all understand it the same way now.
4. Nobody has told me what has been happening since I was away.
5. We will accept that and act on it. (Be careful: it is often said and not meant.)
6. I will make brief contact with you on Monday.
5 or 6 right: good. Fewer: read the article again, then cover the meanings and test yourself.
activities.solo: Cover the right-hand side of the article and work from the phrases alone.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the notice
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. Between what hours are deliveries accepted?
2. When must damage be reported?
3. How often is the notice reviewed?
4. Copy one negative passive sentence.
5. Copy the impersonal passive sentence and say who is not named.
6. How many of the six numbered rules keep a by phrase? Why do you think that is?
activities.answers:
1. Between 07:30 and 16:00.
2. On the day it occurs.
3. Every six months.
4. 'Smoking is not permitted anywhere on the premises, including vehicles.'
5. 'It is understood that some deliveries arrive outside these hours.' Nobody is named as understanding it.
6. Only rule 6 keeps one, naming site staff. The rest are rules that hold whoever is on duty,
   so the doer adds nothing. Rule 6 needs it because the visitor must know WHO will accompany them.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the notice with a pen and underline every is and are before you answer.

quizzes.q: Which is the correct noun phrase?
options: the three-year contract signed last March
the signed last March three-year contract
the contract three-year signed last March
signed last March the three-year contract
quizzes.a: the three-year contract signed last March
quizzes.why: Single words go in front of the noun and whole phrases go behind it. Signed last March is a phrase, so it follows.

quizzes.q: A device was fitted last year and it is faulty. As one phrase: the faulty device ___ last year.
quizzes.why: It is a shortened relative clause: which WAS fitted last year, with the middle removed. The -ed form is what survives.

quizzes.q: Somebody says 'The job went badly.' Which question gets you the most?
quizzes.why: The other three can all be answered with yes or no, which closes the conversation down.

options: Could you tell me where is the venue?
Could you tell me where does the venue?
Could you tell me is the venue where?
Could you tell me where the venue is?
quizzes.a: Could you tell me where the venue is?
quizzes.why: Only the opening is a question. The part after it goes back into statement order, so is follows the venue.

quizzes.q: What does it cost? Politely: Do you know what it ___ ?
quizzes.why: does disappears completely and hands its work back to the main verb, which takes the s again.

quizzes.q: Is it open? Politely: Do you know ___ it is open?
quizzes.why: A yes-or-no question inside needs if or whether to join it on. There is no question word available to use.

quizzes.q: A panel assesses every application. As a rule:
options: Applications is assessed by a panel.
Applications are assess by a panel.
Applications are assessed by a panel.
quizzes.a: Applications are assessed by a panel.
quizzes.why: Applications is plural so are, and assess becomes the participle assessed. The by phrase stays because the reader needs to know who decides.

quizzes.q: Smoking ___ not permitted anywhere on the premises.
quizzes.why: Smoking is one thing, so is; and in a passive the not sits between the two pieces, never in front of them.

quizzes.q: Why do written rules use the passive so heavily?
options: Because a rule must hold whoever is on duty.
quizzes.a: Because a rule must hold whoever is on duty.
quizzes.why: We check every item is only true while we are working. Every item is checked is true always, which is what a rule needs.

quizzes.q: 'It is said that the site will close.' What has the sentence not told you?
quizzes.why: That is the whole property of the impersonal passive. Asking by whom is the skill this unit is teaching.

quizzes.q: Which sentence is missing a doer in a way that MATTERS?
options: Every item is checked against the order.
The site will be cleared before work begins.
The notice is reviewed every six months.
quizzes.a: The site will be cleared before work begins.
quizzes.why: Two parties each assumed the other would do it, so nobody did. In the other three the rule holds whoever is on duty.

quizzes.q: Somebody says they will 'run it past the client'. What will they do?
quizzes.why: It is an idiom, so the individual words do not give the meaning. Ask what the speaker wants from you instead.

teacherNotes.note: The plan's pattern list here was defining relative clauses, non-defining clauses and the comma, and where/whose. All three belong to 7Us.04, placed in Unit 1 and taught there, with L2 U7, U12 and U20 below that. The codes actually placed here are 7Ug.01 (questions that develop an idea), 7Ug.02 (present simple and passive forms) and 7Uv.04 (complex noun phrases). The plan's list has been rewritten to match.

Card 4 increments L2 U16 'Is made, are grown, is sold', which built the same form on a production line. Cards 2 and 3 increment the question work in L1 U1, U7 and U18 and L2 U1 and U15, all of which taught question WORDS rather than follow-up or indirect questions.

Indirect question word order is the hardest item in this unit and it persists well past B1. The version with does is worse than the version with is, because the does has to disappear entirely. Drill card 3 aloud rather than on paper: the wrong order sounds wrong before it looks wrong.
Learners try to stack everything in front of the noun, because many languages allow it. The correction is one sentence: a whole action has to follow the noun.

Complex noun phrases (card 1) are taught nowhere below this unit. Everything else in the unit increments something. If a learner has skipped Level 2, card 1 is the only one that will stand on its own.

Card 5 and Practice 5 teach learners to notice when responsibility has been removed from a sentence. Practice 5 item 6 deliberately shows a missing doer that is entirely proper, so the lesson is judgement rather than suspicion. Do not let the class conclude that every passive hides something.
7Rd.04 (idiomatic phrases) is carried by Reading 2, Practice 6 and quiz item 12 rather than by a pattern card, because an idiom is learned as an item and not as a rule.

selfAssessment.statement: I can build a long noun phrase that holds several facts at once.
I know that single words go in front of the noun and phrases go behind it.
I can ask a follow-up question that cannot be answered with yes or no.
I can ask politely, and put the inside of the question back into statement order.
I can write a rule in the passive so it applies to everybody.
I can spot a sentence that does not say who is responsible.
I can judge whether a missing doer matters or not.
I can work out a workplace idiom from what the speaker wants.

assignment.title: Write the procedure, then take it apart
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write the conditions of entry, or the application procedure, for a place you invent.
Six numbered rules, all passive, at least one negative. Keep by only where a reader needs it.
Use at least three long noun phrases, each with something in front of the noun and a phrase behind it.
Part two. Write six polite enquiries somebody might send about your procedure,
each with a different opening, and two of them using if or whether.
Part three. Read your own rules again and find the one sentence where a reader could
reasonably ask by whom. Rewrite it so they cannot, and say in one sentence what changed.
assignment.submissionType: Written procedure, enquiries and a short analysis
